title: ZIP Codes Within Radius: The Circle's List
description: List every ZIP code whose centroid falls within a radius with ZIP Codes Within Radius — distances shown, ready to copy. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, a 1,000-mile circle around Manhattan's 10001 gathers Boston's 02108 (187.9 mi), Washington's 20001 (204.5), Chicago's 60601 (710.4) and Atlanta's 30303 (747.8) — while Miami's 33101, at 1,094 miles, stays outside.
quick_answer: ZIP Codes Within Radius lists every ZIP code whose centroid falls inside a circle around a centre ZIP or point, each with its distance. Set centre and radius and read the list — the working set for direct mail and territory design, every candidate measured.
steps_intro: The circle, converted into a mailing-grade list:

body.t: A radius campaign needs the codes, not a picture of a circle. This list is the drop, ready to hand to the mail house.
A new territory starts as 'everything within 25 miles of the depot' — the list is that sentence made enumerable, comparable against the
Zones priced by distance bands need the codes per band: run the radius in rings and the pricing table builds itself.
Which codes does a rival's 'local' claim actually cover? The circle's list is the checkable version of the claim.

The summary's four insiders are sorted by distance from 10001's centroid — Chicago (710.4 mi) before Atlanta (747.8) surprises people who think in state shapes instead of straight lines. The list's order is the geometry's, not the atlas's.

A ZIP whose area touches your circle but whose centroid sits outside does not appear — membership is centroid-based, stated plainly. For boundary-sensitive work, widen the radius by the typical ZIP size and trim by hand.

popular_table.note: ZIP 'areas' on maps are Census ZCTAs; centroids are the practical stand-ins every ZIP tool uses. Distances here are centroid-to-centroid — the method's name travels with the list.

faq: Can I centre on an address instead of a ZIP?
Yes — an address or point works as the centre; the ZIP list around it is identical in method. ZIP-to-ZIP is simply the common case.
Both, per this site's convention — radii and distances report in the unit you choose.
How many ZIPs can a list hold?
A 100-mile circle around a metro centre can hold well over a thousand codes. The list handles it; your mail house's pricing will have opinions too.
Codes with centroids in the data participate; a handful of special-purpose codes lack meaningful centroids and are excluded by the method, not by editorial choice.
Can I exclude some returned ZIPs?
The list is yours once produced — trim it in your spreadsheet. Deliberate exclusions beat radius-fiddling, because the record of why stays with you.
Is this the same as ZIPs the circle covers?
No — centroid membership versus area coverage differ at the edges, as the examples state. Boundary-exact coverage belongs to GIS work with ZCTA polygons.
A fair audit technique: your circle, their centre. The geometry does not care whose point it is, and neither does the list.
Why is a visibly-inside ZIP missing?
Its centroid fell outside — check the map view: the code's area reaches in while its centre stays out. The stated convention predicts exactly these cases.
